title: IPMAT Indore VA Full Sectional Mock - Set 12 (Advanced Level)

questions.passage:
Every translator is accused, sooner or later, of betrayal. The Italian pun traduttore, traditore, translator, traitor, has been repeated for so long that it has acquired the weight of a diagnosis. Few other crafts are praised so rarely when they succeed and blamed so readily when they fail. The charge presupposes a simple picture: a text has a meaning, the meaning lives in the words of the original language, and the translator's task is to carry it across without spilling. On this picture every loss is a failure, and the perfect translation, though never achieved, is the one in which the reader forgets that anything has been carried at all.

The picture is old, and so is the dispute about it. Cicero, translating Greek orators into Latin, declared that he had rendered them not as an interpreter but as an orator, keeping the ideas and their form while adapting the idiom to Roman ears. Jerome, centuries later, defended translating sense for sense rather than word for word, except in the case of Scripture, where even the order of the words is a mystery. In 1680 John Dryden proposed a threefold scheme: metaphrase, which turns an author word by word and line by line; paraphrase, in which the author is kept in view but his words are not so strictly followed as his sense; and imitation, in which the translator abandons the original as far as he sees fit. Dryden favoured the middle path, and most later theorists have in some form followed him.

In 1813 the German theologian Friedrich Schleiermacher gave the dispute a sharper shape. There are, he said, only two methods: the translator either leaves the writer in peace as far as possible and moves the reader towards him, or leaves the reader in peace as far as possible and moves the writer towards the reader. The two roads cannot be mixed without confusion. Schleiermacher preferred the first, on the ground that German would be enriched by being stretched towards the foreign. The American theorist Lawrence Venuti revived the distinction in 1995 under the names of domestication and foreignisation. He argued that the dominant Anglo-American tradition, which prizes fluency, renders translators invisible and flattens the foreign text into the idiom of the target culture, and he urged translators to leave visible traces of the original's strangeness.

The case for the opposite emphasis was made most influentially by Eugene Nida, who in the 1960s, working on Bible translation, argued for dynamic equivalence: a translation should aim to produce in its readers the same effect that the original produced in its own. The principle has the merit of practicality. A translator who renders "white as snow" literally for a people who have never seen snow delivers the words but not the meaning. Yet it has its own difficulty, which is that the effect of a text is not a fact that can be read off the page. Readers differ, and the effect on the original's first audience, who shared its assumptions, cannot be recovered. Dynamic equivalence thus tends to replace one uncertain target with another.

Walter Benjamin proposed in 1923 that the debate rested on a mistake. A translation, he argued, is not addressed to readers who do not know the original, and its function is not to communicate. It exists because the original has an afterlife, a continuing existence in another language, and a good translation reveals a kinship among languages that no single language expresses alone. By this standard a translation that reads as if it had been written in the target language is not a success but a disguise.

These abstractions meet practical hazards. The translator of poetry must decide whether to preserve meaning or music: a rhyme scheme carried into English from a language rich in rhyming endings may force padding and distort the sense, while a prose crib preserves content and destroys what made the poem a poem. Edward FitzGerald's celebrated 1859 version of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam took such liberties with its Persian quatrains that critics have disputed whether it is a translation at all, yet it made the poem a fixture of English literature. And there are words that resist transfer, such as the Portuguese saudade, a longing for something absent that may never have existed, for which English offers only a phrase. The choice between phrase and footnote is itself an interpretation.

Translation has also been an instrument of power. When William Jones published his English version of Kalidasa's Shakuntala in 1789, he introduced Sanskrit drama to European readers and won the admiration of Goethe, but the translation also fitted the work to what Europeans expected of the East, and for a generation it stood in for the original. The traffic has long been uneven: a handful of languages, English above all, supply most of what is translated, while many literatures are translated rarely, and often through an intermediary language, so that a text passes through two sets of choices before it reaches its reader.

The arrival of machine translation has sharpened rather than settled the question. Systems trained on vast bodies of text now produce fluent output, and fluency, which the domesticating tradition prized, can be generated at scale. But fluency is exactly the quality that conceals error: a smooth sentence invites trust, and a mistranslation that reads well is more dangerous than a clumsy one that signals its own doubt. A human translator makes a choice and can be asked to justify it; a model's choices are statistical regularities, which cannot.

What follows is not that translation is impossible, but that it is a form of interpretation, and interpretation is answerable to more than one standard. The question to put to a translation is therefore not whether it is faithful, as though fidelity were a single property, but to what it is faithful: the words, the sense, the effect, the form, or the strangeness of the original. Every translation picks among these, and the best make the choice visible.
questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: A) The long dispute between literal and free translation was settled by Dryden's middle path, which later theorists have shown to be correct in all cases.
B) Translation is a form of interpretation answerable to several standards, so the real question is what a translation is faithful to.
C) Machine translation has made human translators obsolete, since fluent output can now be produced at scale and at very little cost to readers.
D) Translation is impossible in the strict sense, because words carry meanings that cannot be carried from one language to another without loss.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The last paragraph says translation is interpretation, answerable to more than one standard, and that the right question is to what a translation is faithful. B overstates Dryden ('settled', 'all cases'); C reverses the point about machine fluency concealing error; D is rejected outright ('not that translation is impossible').

questions.question: The author's description of Schleiermacher's two methods implies that
options: A) Schleiermacher believed that translation into German should be avoided in order to protect the purity of the national language.
B) the first method is better than the second in every circumstance, whatever the nature of the text being translated.
C) Venuti was the first theorist to propose the distinction, which had not been considered by anyone before 1995.
D) a translator must choose whether to move the reader towards the author or the author towards the reader, and cannot do both.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'The two roads cannot be mixed without confusion' means a choice is forced. B contradicts his wish to enrich German through the foreign; C overstates (his preference is reported, not claimed to be universal); D is false, since the passage says Venuti 'revived' the distinction.

questions.question: The author's main criticism of Nida's principle of dynamic equivalence is that
options: A) it requires translators to ignore the meaning of the original text in order to please the readers of the translation.
B) it is impractical, since ideas drawn from Scripture cannot be rendered into other languages at all by translators.
C) the effect of a text on its original audience cannot be recovered, so the target it sets is itself uncertain.
D) it has been abandoned by Bible translators in favour of the word-for-word method that Jerome had defended.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The author grants it 'the merit of practicality' and then says the effect on the first audience 'cannot be recovered', so one uncertain target replaces another. B, C and D misstate or invent claims; Jerome made Scripture an exception, which is not Nida's context.

questions.question: Each of the following is mentioned in the passage as a difficulty or hazard of translation EXCEPT
options: A) a loss of copyright on publication of a translation
B) preserving meaning at the cost of the music of a poem
C) words for which the target language offers only a phrase
D) fluent errors that conceal themselves from the reader
questions.explanation: Explanation: B, C and D appear in paragraphs 6 and 7. Copyright is never mentioned.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken Venuti's claim that the tradition of fluency renders translators invisible?
options: A) Publishers pay translators lower fees than they pay authors, and often omit the translator's name from the cover.
B) Machine translation now produces fluent text in most major languages at a fraction of the cost of human translation.
C) Translations that preserved the foreign flavour of the original were reviewed more favourably than fluent ones in earlier centuries.
D) Most readers of translated novels know the translator's name and regularly compare the translation with the original.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Invisibility means readers do not notice or credit the translator. If readers know the translator and compare versions, the claim is weakened. B supports it, C concerns machines, and D concerns earlier centuries, not the present tradition.

It exists because the original has an afterlife, a continuing existence in another language, and a good translation reveals a kinship among languages that no single language expresses alone. By this standard a translation that reads as if it had been written in the target language is not a success but a disguise.

These abstractions meet practical hazards. The translator of poetry must decide whether to preserve meaning or music: a rhyme scheme carried into English from a language rich in rhyming endings may force padding and distort the sense, while a prose crib preserves content and destroys what made the poem a poem. Edward FitzGerald's celebrated 1859 version of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam took such liberties with its Persian quatrains that critics have disputed whether it is a translation at all, yet it made the poem a fixture of English literature. And there are words that resist transfer, such as the Portuguese saudade, a longing for something absent that may never have existed, for which English offers only a phrase. The choice between phrase and footnote is itself an interpretation.

Translation has also been an instrument of power. When William Jones published his English version of Kalidasa's Shakuntala in 1789, he introduced Sanskrit drama to European readers and won the admiration of Goethe, but the translation also fitted the work to what Europeans expected of the East, and for a generation it stood in for the original. The traffic has long been uneven: a handful of languages, English above all, supply most of what is translated, while many literatures are translated rarely, and often through an intermediary language, so that a text passes through two sets of choices before it reaches its reader.

The arrival of machine translation has sharpened rather than settled the question. Systems trained on vast bodies of text now produce fluent output, and fluency, which the domesticating tradition prized, can be generated at scale. But fluency is exactly the quality that conceals error: a smooth sentence invites trust, and a mistranslation that reads well is more dangerous than a clumsy one that signals its own doubt. A human translator makes a choice and can be asked to justify it; a model's choices are statistical regularities, which cannot.

What follows is not that translation is impossible, but that it is a form of interpretation, and interpretation is answerable to more than one standard. The question to put to a translation is therefore not whether it is faithful, as though fidelity were a single property, but to what it is faithful: the words, the sense, the effect, the form, or the strangeness of the original. Every translation picks among these, and the best make the choice visible.
questions.question: A critic who judged translations by Benjamin's standard would most likely
options: A) praise a translation chiefly for how easily readers unfamiliar with the original could follow it from start to finish.
B) doubt that a translation reading as though written in the target language had done its work.
C) demand that a translation reproduce the effect of the original on its first audience as exactly as is possible.
D) reject translation altogether, since on his view no text has any life beyond the language in which it was written.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage says that by this standard a translation that reads as if written in the target language is 'a disguise'. B contradicts 'its function is not to communicate'; C is Nida's standard; D contradicts the idea of an 'afterlife' in another language.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The candidate's ________ answers, neither confirming nor denying the charge, convinced the panel that she was hiding something.
options: A) forthright
B) categorical
C) evasive
D) lucid
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Evasive' means deliberately avoiding a direct answer. 'Forthright' and 'categorical' describe direct answers, and 'lucid' means clear.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The old professor's reputation rested on a single ________ paper, written in his twenties and never equalled.
options: A) seminal
B) derivative
C) tendentious
D) cursory
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Seminal' means highly influential and original. A 'derivative' or 'cursory' paper could not found a lasting reputation, and 'tendentious' means biased.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The company's apology was dismissed as mere lip service, since ________.
options: A) it was published in the major newspapers on the same day as the announcement of the losses
B) the chief executive had spoken movingly of the suffering of the customers who had been affected
C) it included a detailed timetable for compensating every customer who had been harmed by the faulty product
D) it promised no change in the practices that had caused the harm
questions.explanation: Explanation: Lip service is words without action. Only the first option shows an absence of action. B is about timing, C about sincerity of tone, and D describes real action, which contradicts the criticism.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

The reforms were ________ on paper, but officials with no interest in enforcing them ________ them until nothing was left but a ________ of the original aims.
options: A) timid; hollowed out; shadow
B) sweeping; hollowed out; shadow
C) sweeping; hollowed out; abundance
D) sweeping; fortified; remnant
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Sweeping' on paper, then 'hollowed out' until only a 'shadow' remained. In B, 'timid' removes the contrast with 'but'; C's 'abundance' contradicts 'nothing was left but'; D's 'fortified' contradicts the officials' disinterest.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

Her ________ wit made her popular at dinners but ________ colleagues who felt that she mocked everything they held ________.
options: A) caustic; delighted; dear
B) genial; alienated; dear
C) caustic; alienated; dear
D) caustic; alienated; trivial
questions.explanation: Explanation: Biting ('caustic') wit, which alienated colleagues who felt that she mocked what they held dear. B contradicts 'mocked'; C's 'genial' wit would not mock; D makes the colleagues' own view of things 'trivial', which is illogical.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the portion in square brackets:

No sooner [had the lecture begun when] the lights went out.
options: A) had the lecture begun than
B) the lecture had already begun when
C) did the lecture begin before
D) had the lecture begun then
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'No sooner' takes 'than' and requires the inverted past perfect: 'No sooner had X than Y'. 'When' belongs with 'hardly' or 'scarcely'.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the portion in square brackets:

Neither of the two proposals [were acceptable to the board] because of its cost.
options: A) have been acceptable to the board members
B) were being acceptable to the board
C) are acceptable to the board
D) was acceptable to the board
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Neither' takes a singular verb, and 'its cost' confirms the singular. The sentence is also in the past tense, which 'are' and 'have been' fail to match.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'We usually imagine memory as a recording, which can be replayed accurately if only we concentrate. ________ Each time a memory is recalled, it is reconstructed from fragments and can be altered by the circumstances of recall, so that confident recollections of events, such as the details of a crime witnessed years ago, are often wrong. Confidence, moreover, is a poor guide to accuracy.'
options: A) Memories fade because the brain, like a tape, wears out the more often it is played back.
B) The evidence, however, suggests that memory is closer to a reconstruction than to a recording.
C) Psychologists agree that people who recall events with great confidence are almost always correct.
D) Witnesses should be trained to concentrate harder, since effort is the only factor that determines accuracy of recall.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The blank must reject the recording picture and set up the reconstruction described next. B keeps the tape metaphor; C contradicts 'confidence is a poor guide'; D contradicts the claim that recall itself alters memory.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'An insurer who offers cover at a single price attracts mainly those who know they are the most likely to claim. ________ As the healthy leave, the pool grows sicker, premiums rise, and more of the healthy leave, until the market may collapse. This is the problem of adverse selection.'
options: A) Healthy customers, by contrast, are eager to buy cover at any price, since they value security above all else.
B) Insurers therefore refuse to sell cover to anyone who has ever made a claim on a policy of any kind.
C) Those who expect to claim little find the price poor value and decline to buy.
D) Governments have always provided such cover directly, since private insurers cannot operate profitably in any market.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The following sentence begins 'As the healthy leave', so the blank must explain why they leave. B says the opposite; C and D introduce unrelated claims.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The stationary supplier delivered the pens and paper a week late.
B) The committee will proceed to vote once the chairman has summarised the arguments of each side.
C) Her lawyer will counsel her against signing the agreement until the terms have been clarified.
D) The rise in prices did not precede the shortage but followed it, as the data clearly show.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Stationery' means paper and writing materials; 'stationary' means not moving. 'Proceed', 'counsel' (advise) and 'precede' are used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The treasurer will disperse the funds to each department on Monday morning.
B) The detective's question was meant to elicit a confession from the suspect.
C) The thief managed to elude the police for nearly three weeks after the robbery.
D) The speaker did not name the scandal but alluded to it in passing.
questions.explanation: Explanation: To 'disburse' is to pay out money; 'disperse' means to scatter. 'Alluded' (referred indirectly), 'elicit' (draw out) and 'elude' (escape) are all correct.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. This is why nineteenth-century portraits look so stiff and solemn.
2. Smiling, which is hard to hold for minutes, became common in photographs only afterwards.
3. Early photographers were advised to keep their subjects perfectly still, since exposures could last several minutes.
4. When faster lenses and more sensitive plates shortened exposures to a fraction of a second, the stiffness began to disappear.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 states the old condition (long exposures). 1 ('This is why') explains the stiff look. 4 ('When faster lenses...') gives the change, and 2 ('afterwards') draws the consequence for smiling. Order: 3-1-4-2.

questions.passage:
Interviewer: Dr Menon, cities keep widening roads, and congestion seems to return within a few years. Why?

Dr Menon: Because of what we call induced demand. A wider road lowers the cost of driving, in time, and when something gets cheaper people do more of it: they take trips they would have skipped, they switch from buses, or they move farther from work. The new capacity fills until congestion returns to roughly where it started. Notice that this does not mean the new road is worthless, because people are making more trips, and that has value. What it means is that the promised benefit, faster journeys, evaporates.

Interviewer: So we shouldn't build roads?

Dr Menon: I wouldn't go that far. In a city with genuinely missing links, a new road can help. My objection is to treating congestion as a shortage of road, when it is a shortage of something else: a price for using road space at peak times. Cities that charge for entry to the centre, as London and Stockholm do, have seen traffic fall and, importantly, stay down. The politics is hard, because drivers see the charge and not the time they save.
questions.question: According to Dr Menon, widening roads fails to end congestion because
options: A) drivers refuse to use the new capacity, since they regard the charge for using it as unfairly high.
B) cheaper driving induces more trips, until congestion returns to roughly its earlier level.
C) the new roads are usually built in the wrong places, so that they fail to connect the areas that need them most.
D) buses and other forms of public transport become faster than cars, and so travellers abandon their vehicles in large numbers.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Induced demand: lower cost of driving leads to more trips, filling the new capacity. The other options contradict this or invent claims.

questions.question: Dr Menon's stance on road building is best described as
options: A) opposed: she holds that no new road in any city can ever deliver a benefit to the people who use it.
B) supportive: she believes that wider roads, once built, permanently solve the problem of congestion in cities.
C) conditional: roads can help where links are missing, but congestion calls for pricing rather than more capacity.
D) neutral: she regards the question of whether to build roads as a matter of political preference and nothing more.
questions.explanation: Explanation: She says new roads can help 'where links are missing' but that congestion is a shortage of a price, not of road. B and C are extreme; D contradicts her substantive arguments.
